data.title: Discovery — how context is handed to AI, how we do it, and how people sync their work
body: # Discovery — how context is handed to AI, how we do it, and how people sync their work
- **Method:** desk research (Tavily), 4 queries + reading the sources; our own part verified locally
- **Decision it supports:** whether the form in which kadence hands over context (a journal in the repository + a CLI) is the right one for teams of 3–8 — and what to change
- **Marks:** **Fact** · **Finding** · **Assumption**
## 1. How context is usually handed to AI
### 1.1 The discipline changed its name, and that is not cosmetic

Prompt engineering has been displaced by **context engineering** — the design of everything the model sees on every call: the system frame, tool definitions, retrieved documents, history, memory between sessions — **Fact** ([Sourcegraph](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/context-engineering), [Faros](https://www.faros.ai/blog/context-engineering-for-developers)).

The reason is concrete: every frontier model **measurably degrades as the context grows, long before the window is full**. The remedy is not a bigger window but a disciplined budget — **Fact** ([Crux Digits](https://cruxdigits.nl/blog/context-engineering-ai-agents-2026)).

A signal that this already costs money: in July 2026 Amazon shipped CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights — a separate product for monitoring how agents work inside an organisation, with telemetry from Claude Code, Codex and Copilot. Vendors do not build monitoring for problems that cost nobody anything — **Fact** (same source) + **Finding** as to the interpretation.
### 1.2 Four loading levels
The settled split: **always-loaded · on-demand · delegated · automated** — **Fact** ([Bitloops](https://bitloops.com/resources/context-engineering)).

The rule for the first level: keep the system frame **under ~2,000 tokens** and push everything else down to the appropriate level. The typical mistake is to stuff into ambient everything the agent "might need": that spends tokens on information needed in 10% of cases and **pushes what actually matters further from the model's attention** — **Fact** ([Taskade](https://www.taskade.com/blog/context-engineering)).
### 1.3 Give a way to fetch, rather than guessing in advance

The ReAct pattern and just-in-time retrieval: instead of cramming everything in up front — give the agent tools to fetch what it needs itself. This shifts the task from "predict everything that will be needed" to "give a way to get it". The price is more calls and latency — **Fact** ([Firecrawl](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/context-engineering)).
### 1.4 Structural context against semantic

The distinction that concerns us most: structural context says **what** the code does; semantic says **why** it exists and which trade-offs were taken. The source's formulation: agents without semantic context are pattern-matchers; with it they are the ones who make decisions — **Fact** ([Bitloops](https://bitloops.com/resources/context-engineering)).
### 1.5 Metadata against silent rot

The recommendation is to put a header with `last_updated`, `owner`, `scope`, `reviewed_by` into context files. Useful twice over: the agent understands whether this is worth reading (progressive disclosure), and a human in six months knows whom to ask when the file looks out of date — **Fact** ([Packmind](https://packmind.com/context-engineering-ai-coding/context-engineering-best-practices)).
## 2. How we do it
Verified locally on a fresh `kadence init` (2026-09-08), not from memory.
| Level | What we have | Size |
| **Always-loaded** | the section in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` | **593 B ≈ 148 tokens** |
| **On-demand** | `.kadence/README.md` | 1,887 B |
| **On-demand** | `kadence schema --json` | 3,482 B |
| **On-demand** | `task show --json` | **948 B, constant** regardless of project size |
| **Delegated** | — | none |
| **Automated** | — | none |
**What matches best practice — Finding:**

1. **An ambient layer of 148 tokens against a recommended ceiling of 2,000.** We are an order of magnitude below the limit, and that is not an accident: the section points at a command instead of describing the contract in prose.

2. **Progressive disclosure is implemented exactly as ReAct.** We do not predict what the agent will need — we give it `schema --json`, `task show --json`, `--fields`. That is precisely what §1.3 calls the more reliable approach.
3. **`task show --json` — 948 bytes regardless of history** ([Probe C](DOC-57)). A disciplined budget is not a slogan but a guardrail test.
**Three gaps — Finding:**
| Gap | Consequence |

| **No semantic context.** The journal says what happened and when. It does not say **why** it was done this way and what was rejected | By the definition in §1.4 our agent remains a pattern-matcher. That is exactly what `kadence decision` is meant to close — and this is already the second independent source pointing at the same hole |

| **No metadata in the files we write into someone else's repository.** No `last_updated`, no version, no source — verified: zero matches | In a year nobody will know whether the section in `AGENTS.md` is current or where it came from. We are creating exactly the silent drift §1.5 warns about — and we are doing it in other people's repositories |

| **No delegated and automated levels.** Everything rests on the agent deciding to call the CLI itself | If it does not call, it gets nothing. We have no mechanism at all that delivers context without the agent's initiative |
## 3. Small teams

There is little direct data, and that should be recorded honestly: a search for "small teams and process overhead" returned mostly tool round-ups rather than research — **Fact** about the quality of the sample.
What could be extracted:

- For a team of 6–8 people the recommendation is **the simplest thing**: stickers and a board, or a spreadsheet where an engineer keeps a list of tasks and estimates and the rest counts itself. The key point is very low overhead for the engineer — **Fact** ([Hugh Williams](https://hughewilliams.com/2012/06/05/6-secrets-for-successful-small-teams), a source from 2012 — **old**, and that is worth taking into account).

- An estimate of the limit: a spreadsheet holds up to about **5 people and 15 active tasks**, beyond which the cost of coordination exceeds the value of tracking — **Fact**, but the source is marketing ([worksbuddy](https://worksbuddy.ai/blogs/what-is-the-best-project-tracker-for-small-teams)), so the number is a guide, not a measurement.

- Teams change tracker not because they want a new tool but because the hidden cost of coordination shows up as slower reviews and blurred ownership — **Fact** ([thisandthat](https://www.thisandthat.chat/blog/engineering-team-task-tracking-statistics)).

**What this means for us — Finding.** Our segment of 3–8 sits exactly in the zone where the spreadsheet is already cracking and Jira is still excessive. This confirms the choice of segment and **says nothing** about whether an event journal is the right form for it. Data about team size and data about the need for our mechanics are different data.
## 4. How to sync work between people
The highest-quality source in the whole study is a practitioner who runs distributed teams.

The gain in productivity comes not from monitoring but from **removing the cost of coordination**, and it consists of exactly three things — **Fact** ([slavikdev](https://slavikdev.com/successful-remote-team)):

1. **Decisions written down where they can be found** — not in Slack threads that scroll into oblivion within hours. For what matters — RFCs and ADRs. The discipline of writing forces a clarity that a spoken conversation avoids, and it creates an artefact that a new team member will find six months later instead of reconstructing the context from someone else's memory.

2. **Status is visible without asking.** "What did you do yesterday?" at a standup is a poor man's visibility system. If a manager has to ask an engineer what they are working on, that is a failure of the system, not of the people.
3. **Fewer meetings that exist only to pass on information a document could have delivered.**

And separately, from a competitor's blog (Plane): coordination becomes simpler when people and agents work **from a shared record of the work** — tasks, context, decisions, ownership and history have to stay linked, so that whoever acts next understands what has already happened — **Fact** ([Plane](https://plane.so/blog/human-ai-collaboration-how-teams-divide-work-with-agents)).
**How we sit against these three — Finding:**
| Condition | kadence |
| Status visible without asking | ✅ `board`, `sprint status`, and the state folds from the events, so it cannot diverge from reality |
| Fewer meetings for the sake of passing on information | ✅ velocity and time spent are derived from the journal, nobody fills in a form |
| **Decisions written down where they will be found** | ❌ **we cannot do it** |

The third row is the same hole as in §2, and now it is confirmed from another side: it is needed **not only by agents but by people too**, and it is precisely the one named as the first condition of cheap coordination.
## 5. What this changes
| # | Action | Rests on |

| 1 | **Metadata in the files `init` writes** — the kadence version, the date, where it came from. Cheap, and without it we create silent drift in other people's repositories | §1.5 + verified that the metadata is zero |

| 2 | **`kadence decision` confirmed a third time, and no longer only for agents.** Semantic context (§1.4), "decisions where they will be found" (§4), and the [discovery about the format](DOC-44) point at one and the same omission | §1.4, §4 |
| 3 | **Do not build the delegated/automated levels.** They need a daemon or a hook, that is a background process — which contradicts "no server". A deliberate boundary, not an oversight | §1.2 |
| 4 | **Add a question to Probe B about recording decisions for **people**, not only for agents** | §4 |
Point 1 is the only one here that is not gated by Probe B: it fixes something we already do in other people's repositories.
## What this research did not answer

**The main thing.** Everything above is about how to hand over context **correctly**. No source said that teams of 3–8 want a **task tracker** to do it. Practitioners describe a context layer, rules files, memory layers — and none of them is a journal of work.

The data about small teams turned out to be the weakest part: one source from 2012 and one marketing one. If the positioning rests on "for small teams", there is currently no research foundation under it — **Assumption**, and one worth checking separately.
And a caveat about the sample: all the sources in §1 are from companies that sell context layers. They are primary about their own products and interested parties about the problem itself.
